script.title: How tax brackets actually work, with real math
script.hook: $60,000 salary, and you pay about 8% of it in federal income tax, not 22%. Here's the real math.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Sixty thousand dollar salary, and the federal income tax works out to about eight percent of it, not twenty-two. If that surprises you, you're not alone. Tax brackets are one of the most misunderstood things in personal finance, and the misunderstanding makes people turn down raises and overtime. In this video we'll do the real math on a simple example, step by step, using 2026 numbers for a single filer. Check the IRS tables for your year before relying on exact figures.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes at a whiteboard with a staircase drawing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1
segments.narration: Step one: start with income. Our example earns sixty thousand dollars in wages, nothing else. No traditional 401(k) contributions yet, to keep it simple.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single tall coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2
segments.narration: Step two: subtract the standard deduction. For 2026 returns that's about sixteen thousand one hundred for a single filer. Sixty thousand minus sixteen thousand one hundred leaves forty-three thousand nine hundred of taxable income. So right away, over a quarter of the income isn't taxed at all.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a shield covering the bottom of the coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3
segments.narration: Step three: fill the brackets like buckets. The first twelve thousand four hundred of taxable income is taxed at ten percent. That's twelve hundred forty dollars. The rest, from twelve thousand four hundred up to forty-three thousand nine hundred, is thirty-one thousand five hundred, taxed at twelve percent. That's three thousand seven hundred eighty.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two stacked buckets, the bottom one full, the second partly full. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4
segments.narration: Step four: add them up. Twelve forty plus thirty-seven eighty is five thousand twenty dollars of federal income tax. Divide by sixty thousand and the effective rate is about eight point four percent. This person's top bracket is twelve percent, but they pay eight point four percent overall.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small coin pile next to a big one with a percent tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The raise myth
segments.narration: Now the myth. People say 'I don't want a raise, it'll push me into a higher bracket.' A higher bracket only applies to the dollars above the line. If this person's taxable income crossed into the twenty-two percent bracket, only the dollars past fifty thousand four hundred would be taxed at twenty-two. Every dollar below keeps its lower rate. A raise always increases take-home pay from income tax alone.
segments.on_screen_text: Higher bracket = only the extra dollars
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a staircase where only the top step changes color. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 401(k) effect
segments.narration: Here's where it gets useful. Say they put six percent, thirty-six hundred dollars, into a traditional 401(k). That comes out before income tax, so taxable income drops to forty thousand three hundred. At twelve percent, that saves about four hundred thirty dollars of tax. The paycheck shrinks by less than the amount saved, because the tax break covers part of it.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin dropping into a jar before a tax gate, a small coin returning. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: A raise, worked out
segments.narration: Let's test the raise myth with numbers. Our example gets a raise from sixty thousand to seventy thousand. Taxable income goes from forty-three thousand nine hundred to fifty-three thousand nine hundred. The twelve percent bracket ends at about fifty thousand four hundred, so most of the raise is taxed at twelve percent, and only the last thirty-five hundred dollars at twenty-two. Federal income tax goes from five thousand twenty to about sixty-five hundred seventy. The ten-thousand-dollar raise adds about fifteen hundred fifty dollars of federal income tax, and they keep about eighty-four fifty of it, before payroll and state taxes. The effective rate moves from about eight point four percent to about nine point four. Nobody ends up with less money after a raise.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two bar stacks, one slightly taller. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your own numbers in four lines
segments.narration: To do this for yourself, you need four lines on a piece of paper. Line one: your expected income for the year. Line two: minus the standard deduction, or your itemized deductions if they're bigger, and minus traditional 401(k) contributions. Line three: fill the brackets from the bottom, using this year's numbers from IRS dot gov. Line four: subtract any credits. Then divide line four by line one for your effective rate. It takes about ten minutes, and it makes every tax headline easier to understand.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a sheet of paper with four lines. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Bonuses feel different
segments.narration: One more thing people notice: a bonus check can look heavily taxed. That's usually withholding, not a higher tax rate. Employers often withhold a flat twenty-two percent on bonuses for federal tax. If your real bracket is twelve percent, the extra withheld generally comes back as part of your refund when you file. The tax on the bonus is the same as on any other wages.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a bonus check with a small arrow back. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credits vs deductions
segments.narration: Deductions, like that 401(k) contribution, reduce taxable income, so their value depends on your bracket. Credits reduce the tax itself, dollar for dollar. A five-hundred-dollar Saver's Credit cuts five hundred off the five thousand twenty. That's why credits like the Saver's Credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit are worth checking even when the deduction math feels small.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. scissors cutting a bill next to a small slice off a coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Withholding
segments.narration: And your paycheck withholding is an estimate of all this, spread across the year. If you get a big refund every year, withholding is set too high. If you owe, it's too low. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator lines the two up. This is also why a bonus can look over-taxed on the stub: it's often withheld at a flat rate, and the real tax is settled when you file.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck with a small slice going to an envelope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State and payroll taxes
segments.narration: Two things this example left out. State income tax, which ranges from zero in some states to several percent in others. And payroll taxes: Social Security and Medicare, seven point six five percent of wages, which don't have the standard deduction and aren't bracketed the same way. So the total tax picture is bigger than income tax, but the bracket logic is the same.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two small extra slices on a coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Subtract the standard deduction first. Fill the brackets like buckets from the bottom. Your effective rate is far lower than your top bracket. A raise never lowers take-home because of brackets. Traditional 401(k) contributions save tax at your top rate. Credits cut tax dollar for dollar. And withholding is just an estimate you can adjust.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes pointing at the full staircase with a smile. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Rate My Budget: a teacher, a retail worker and a $90K renter
script.hook: 3 more budgets, 3 more scores out of 10, and the fixes with real numbers.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Three more budgets, three more scores out of ten, and the fixes with real numbers. As always, these are fictional examples built from common patterns, not real people. We score on five questions, two points each: savings rate, housing share, high-rate debt, irregular costs, and automation. Grab your own numbers and score along.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes with a clipboard in front of three small buildings. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 1
segments.narration: Budget one: a teacher earning fifty-five thousand, paid over ten months, about thirty-eight hundred a month take-home. Rent thirteen hundred, car three hundred, loans two hundred. Every summer, about six thousand of living costs goes on a credit card. Scores: savings zero, housing two at thirty-four percent, debt zero because the card balance recurs, irregular zero, automation one. Three out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with two blank summer months. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 1
segments.narration: The fix: the summer gap divided by ten paychecks. Six thousand over ten is six hundred a month into a separate summer account. If the district offers twelve-month pay, that does it automatically. The card stops growing every summer, which saves a few hundred dollars of interest a year. New score: seven, then eight once a small regular savings transfer starts.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar filling across ten months and pouring out in summer. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 2
segments.narration: Budget two: a retail worker earning forty-one thousand, about thirteen hundred every two weeks. Rent is eleven hundred and due on the first, but some paydays land on the third. Result: about three overdrafts a month at thirty-five dollars each, a hundred and five a month, over twelve hundred a year in fees. Scores: savings zero, housing one, debt two, irregular zero, automation zero. Three out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small fee tags stacking on a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 2
segments.narration: The fix costs nothing. Ask the landlord to move the due date to the fifth. Move other bills after paydays too. Turn on low-balance alerts, and opt out of overdraft coverage on debit card purchases so they decline instead of costing thirty-five dollars. Then the hundred and five a month that used to go to fees builds a one-week buffer in about three months. New score: seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar date being dragged later and a cushion filling. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 3
segments.narration: Budget three: ninety thousand a year, about fifty-four hundred take-home. Rent twenty-four hundred, a car payment of eleven hundred plus two hundred insurance. That's thirty-seven hundred, sixty-eight percent of take-home, on two things. Savings is a hundred a month. Scores: savings one, housing one at forty-four percent, debt two, irregular zero, automation one. Five out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a tall apartment and a shiny car squeezing a tiny jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 3
segments.narration: The fix is about the biggest lines, not lattes. Plan to sell the car and buy a reliable used one with a payment around four hundred, or refinance if the rate is high. That frees about seven hundred a month, eighty-four hundred a year. At the next lease renewal, set a ceiling: rent plus car under about forty-five percent of take-home. New score: eight.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a car icon shrinking as a jar grows. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Teacher, after six months
segments.narration: Let's check on the fixes with the numbers. Six months after the teacher starts the six-hundred-dollar summer transfer, the summer account holds thirty-six hundred. By June, after ten paychecks, it holds six thousand, which covers July and August without the card. The card balance, which used to grow by about six thousand each summer, stays flat. That's hundreds of dollars of card interest a year that never builds up. Once summer is covered, a hundred dollars a month of regular savings starts, and the score goes to eight. The fix was one transfer and one calendar note, and it repeats every year.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with ten small coins and a sun. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retail worker and renter, after six months
segments.narration: The retail worker's fix is even faster. With the rent due date moved to the fifth and overdraft coverage off, the hundred-and-five-dollar monthly fee bill disappears. After three months, three hundred fifteen dollars sits in savings as a one-week buffer. After six months, it's over six hundred. For the ninety-thousand-dollar renter, the cheaper car frees about seven hundred a month. Six months later, that's forty-two hundred dollars: enough for a starter emergency fund and a few sinking funds. Three different budgets, and in each one the biggest change came from the largest line or a broken system. Small treats weren't the problem in any of them.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two small jars filling side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The scorecard, before and after
segments.narration: Here are all three scores side by side. The teacher went from three to eight. The retail worker went from three to seven. The ninety-thousand-dollar renter went from five to eight. Two of the three fixes cost nothing at all: a monthly transfer and a new rent due date. The third needed a car sale, but freed the most money. Before you cut anything small, check the calendar, the due dates and the two biggest lines in your budget.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a scorecard with three rising scores. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your weakest question
segments.narration: To use this on your own budget, score yourself on the five questions and find your lowest one. If it's savings, set a small automatic transfer, even twenty-five dollars, the day after payday. If it's housing, plan for the next lease renewal now. If it's debt, write down a payoff order. If it's irregular costs, start one sinking fund for the cost that surprises you most. If it's automation, set up one autopay this week. One question at a time.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a scorecard with one row highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pattern
segments.narration: Pattern across all three: none of them needed to give up small pleasures first. The teacher needed a calendar fix, the retail worker needed due dates moved, and the ninety-thousand earner needed to shrink the two biggest bills. Find your biggest structural problem before cutting coffee.

script.title: 401(k), IRA or HSA: which account gets your money first?
script.hook: 3 accounts, 3 tax breaks, and one order that works for most people. Here's the real math.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Three accounts, three different tax breaks, and one order that works for most people starting out. A 401(k), an IRA and an HSA can all cut your taxes, but in different ways. In this video we'll compare them with real numbers, then put them in an order you can follow. General education, not personal advice, and check this year's limits on irs.gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes in front of three jars with different stars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The 401(k)
segments.narration: The 401(k): through your employer, money comes straight from your paycheck. Traditional contributions lower your taxable income now. Roth 401(k) contributions don't, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free. The big feature is the match. If your employer matches fifty cents on the dollar up to six percent, every dollar you put in up to that point gets an instant fifty percent return.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two coins dropping in for every one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The IRA
segments.narration: The IRA: an account you open yourself at a brokerage. Roth IRA contributions are after-tax, grow tax-free, and your contributions, not earnings, can be withdrawn anytime without tax or penalty. Traditional IRA contributions may be deductible depending on income and whether you have a workplace plan. The big feature is choice: you pick from almost any low-cost fund, not just your plan's menu.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar with many small fund icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The HSA
segments.narration: The HSA: only if you have an HSA-eligible health plan. Contributions are pre-tax or deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical costs are tax-free. Three tax breaks in one. Unlike an FSA, it rolls over and stays yours if you change jobs. Through payroll, HSA contributions can also skip Social Security and Medicare tax, which a 401(k) doesn't.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar with three gold stars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Real math
segments.narration: Real math. Fifty thousand salary, twelve percent bracket, a fifty-percent match up to six percent. Putting six percent, three thousand, into the 401(k) gets fifteen hundred from the employer and saves about three hundred sixty of federal tax. Three thousand of your money becomes forty-five hundred invested, at a paycheck cost of about twenty-six forty. That's hard to beat anywhere.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small pile turning into a bigger pile. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Roth vs traditional
segments.narration: Roth or traditional? The rule of thumb is about your tax rate now versus later. Early in your career, in the ten or twelve percent bracket, paying tax now with Roth is often attractive, because you may be in a higher bracket later. In higher brackets, traditional often wins. If you genuinely can't tell, splitting between both is a reasonable answer.
segments.on_screen_text: Low bracket now? Roth often wins
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two jars with tax gates at opposite ends. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The order
segments.narration: So here's the common order. One: contribute to the 401(k) up to the full match. Two: if you have an HSA-eligible plan, fund the HSA, especially through payroll. Three: fund a Roth IRA, if you're under the income limit. Four: go back and raise your 401(k) contribution. Five: after that, a regular brokerage account. Paying off high-interest card debt usually fits between steps one and two.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. five numbered jars in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Worked example: $525 a month, in order
segments.narration: Here's the order with fictional numbers. A fifty-thousand-dollar salary, twelve percent bracket, a fifty percent match up to six percent, and an HSA-eligible health plan. Five hundred twenty-five dollars a month to put away. First, six percent to the 401(k): two hundred fifty a month, and the match adds a hundred twenty-five. Second, a hundred fifty a month to the HSA through payroll. Payroll HSA contributions generally skip income tax and Social Security and Medicare tax, so at twelve plus seven point six five percent, that's about three hundred fifty dollars a year less tax. Third, a hundred twenty-five a month to a Roth IRA. Every dollar has a home, in the order that gives the biggest tax break first.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three labelled boxes filling in order. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Only $100 a month?
segments.narration: Only have a hundred dollars a month? Then it all goes to step one. If six percent of your pay is more than a hundred dollars, contribute what you can and raise it one percent at a time, maybe with each raise. If your employer doesn't match, many people start with a Roth IRA, for the flexibility and the fund choice. The order stays the same whatever the amount. You fill the next box only when the one before it is full.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single box with a small coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Changing jobs
segments.narration: When you change jobs, don't cash out the 401(k). That usually means income tax plus a ten percent penalty if you're under fifty-nine and a half, and it loses years of growth. You can usually leave it in the old plan, move it to the new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA. A direct rollover, where the money goes straight from one provider to the other, avoids withholding problems. Your HSA is yours to keep too, even if you leave the job or change health plans.
segments.on_screen_text: Job change: roll it over, don't cash out
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a box moving between two buildings. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Checking your own plan
segments.narration: To set this up yourself, log into your benefits portal and find three things: your match formula, whether your health plan is HSA-eligible, and your current contribution rate. Most people can find all three in about ten minutes. Write them down, then fill the boxes in order.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a laptop with three small boxes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fees and funds
segments.narration: Whichever account, the investment inside matters. A target-date fund or a broad low-cost index fund works for most beginners. Check the expense ratio. And make sure money is actually invested; IRAs and HSAs often start in cash until you choose something.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin turning into a sprout, scissors on fees. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Common mistakes: skipping the match while saving elsewhere. Using the HSA like a checking account when you could afford to let it grow. Leaving IRA money in cash. And contributing over the limit, which has a penalty. Check the current limits on irs.gov each year.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short list with warning triangles. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Get the full 401(k) match first. If you're HSA-eligible, the HSA's triple tax break is next. Then a Roth IRA, especially in a low bracket. Then raise your 401(k). Pay off high-interest debt early in the sequence. And make sure every account is actually invested in something low-cost.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes checking off five jars. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Money and relationships: how to combine finances without fighting
script.hook: 3 ways to split bills, 1 account setup, and the money talk most couples avoid. Here's the complete guide.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Money is one of the most common things couples argue about, and most of those arguments are really about not having a plan. In this video: when to have the money talk, what to share, three ways to split bills with real math, account setups, debts and credit, big-purchase rules, a monthly money date, and the red flags to take seriously. Whether you're dating, moving in or married, there's a step here for you.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two piggy banks on a park bench. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When to talk
segments.narration: When to talk: before any shared financial commitment. Before a shared lease, a joint account, a shared car or a big trip. You don't need to share everything on a third date, but by the time money is shared, both of you should know the basics. A calm time beats right after a big purchase.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with a small heart before a key icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What to share
segments.narration: What to share: take-home pay, fixed costs, debts with their balances, rates and payments, savings, and credit scores. Swap at the same time so it feels like information, not a confession. If it's hard to start, pull your free credit reports together and use them as the agenda.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two notebooks being swapped. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Splitting: 3 ways
segments.narration: Three ways to split. Fifty-fifty: simple, fair when incomes are close. By income: each pays the same percentage of their pay. All in one pot: everything joint, decided together. Example by income: one takes home forty-two hundred, the other twenty-eight hundred. That's sixty and forty. With twenty-four hundred of shared bills, they pay fourteen-forty and nine-sixty, and both keep about two-thirds of their pay.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three seesaws in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: $2,400 of shared bills, split by income

segments.heading: Accounts
segments.narration: Accounts: the most common setup is yours, mine and ours. A joint account for shared bills and goals, funded each payday by an agreed amount, and personal accounts for everything else, no explanations needed. Add a joint savings account for shared goals. Remember, either owner can usually withdraw everything from a joint account, so trust matters.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two small jars and one big shared jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Debts and credit
segments.narration: Debts and credit: there's no joint credit score. Each of you keeps your own report, even when married. Debts from before the relationship generally stay with their owner, though some states have community property rules. But joint accounts, co-signed loans and authorized-user cards show up on both reports, so a missed payment hurts both. Only co-sign what you could afford to pay yourself.
segments.on_screen_text: No joint score · joint accounts hit both
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two separate score dials with one shared card between. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Big purchases
segments.narration: Big purchases: agree on a dollar amount above which you check in before buying. Two hundred, five hundred, whatever fits. It's not about permission, it's about no surprises. And plan big shared costs, like trips and furniture, as sinking funds you both feed.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a price tag with a small bell. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Worked example: splitting by income
segments.narration: Here's the difference the split makes, with fictional numbers. Partner A takes home four thousand dollars a month, partner B twenty-five hundred. Shared bills are thirty-two hundred fifty. Split fifty-fifty, each pays sixteen twenty-five. A keeps twenty-three seventy-five, and B keeps eight seventy-five, about a third of their pay. Split by income, the shared bills are fifty percent of their combined sixty-five hundred, so each pays half their own pay: A pays two thousand and B pays twelve fifty. Now each keeps exactly half of what they earn. Neither split is wrong. But when incomes are far apart, splitting by income usually feels fairer to both people.
segments.on_screen_text: 50/50: B keeps $875 · by income: both keep 50%
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two piggy banks, one larger, splitting a bill. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Different money habits
segments.narration: Most couples have one saver and one spender, or one planner and one avoider. That isn't a problem to fix; it's two habits to plan around. The personal accounts in yours, mine and ours are what make it work. Each person's fun money is theirs, with no explaining needed. The shared plan covers the bills and the goals you both agreed on. Arguments usually start when one person's habits quietly decide the shared money. Agree on the shared numbers together, then leave each other's personal spending alone.
segments.on_screen_text: Shared plan together · personal money is personal
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two different wallets beside one shared jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Shared goals
segments.narration: Finally, pick one shared goal with a number and a date. An emergency fund of five thousand dollars by next December, or a trip in August that costs eighteen hundred. Divide it by the months until the date, and fund it automatically from the joint account. Eighteen hundred over nine months is two hundred a month, about a hundred each, or split by income. Watching a shared goal grow at each money date is one of the easiest ways to turn money talks into something you both look forward to.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a jar with a small plane label. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When one income changes
segments.narration: Incomes change: a new job, a layoff, parental leave or going back to school. When they do, revisit the split at your next money date. With a split by income, the math adjusts on its own, because each person still pays the same percentage of what they bring in. With fifty-fifty, you'll usually need a new conversation. Agree in advance that the split gets reviewed whenever either income changes.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two piggy banks with a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Money date
segments.narration: The habit that holds it together: a monthly money date. Same day each month, fifteen to twenty minutes. Look at shared bills, progress on goals, anything coming up next month, and one thing you're proud of. Keep it short and pleasant, with a coffee or a dessert. Couples who talk about money regularly fight about it less.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with a heart and two mugs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Red flags
segments.narration: Red flags to take seriously: hiding debts or accounts, pressure to lend money or co-sign, controlling all the money or your access to it, and running up debt in your name. Financial control can be a form of abuse. If that's happening, the National Domestic Violence Hotline has free, confidential support.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small red flags and a shield. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Talk before money is shared. Share pay, debts, savings and scores at the same time. Pick a split: fifty-fifty, by income or one pot. Use yours, mine and ours accounts. Remember there's no joint credit score, but joint accounts hit both. Set a check-in amount for big purchases. Hold a monthly money date. And take the red flags seriously.

Combining finances without fighting:
1. Talk before money is shared
2. Share pay, debts, savings, scores (at the same time)
3. Split 50/50, by income, or one pot (example: 60/40 incomes, $2,400 bills → $1,440 / $960)
4. Yours, mine, ours accounts
5. No joint credit score, but joint accounts hit both reports
6. Check-in amount for big purchases
7. Monthly 15-minute money date
